headings.title: Introduction and Importance of Needle Counting
headings.content: Retained surgical items represent a preventable medical error with devastating consequences for patient health and hospital liability. Needle counting serves as a primary defensive barrier during invasive procedures, protecting patients from internal organ perforation, chronic pain, and secondary infections. In busy Nigerian surgical suites, where resource constraints can sometimes stretch personnel thin, maintaining rigorous counting protocols remains non-negotiable. Every sharp entering the sterile field must be accounted for from skin incision to skin closure. Skipping this routine under the pressure of a fast-paced emergency list invites severe clinical complications and medico-legal exposure.

headings.title: Roles and Responsibilities of the Surgical Team
headings.content: Accurate needle counting relies on clear communication and a shared division of labor between the scrub nurse and the circulating nurse. The scrub nurse manages the sterile field, keeping track of items handed to the surgeon and received back. The circulating nurse remains unsterile, recording every count on the white board or designated institutional sheet as it is called out aloud. Both nurses must visualize the items together during every count phase. Silence or rushed murmurs during this process are unacceptable. If a discrepancy arises, both team members hold equal responsibility to halt the procedure immediately.

headings.title: Standard Protocols and Timing for Counts
headings.content:
A complete surgical count follows a strict temporal sequence throughout an operation. 

- **Initial Count**: Performed before the procedure begins, establishing the baseline inventory of all needles, blades, and sponges while packages are still intact.
- **First Intraoperative Count**: Conducted when the surgeon begins closing a cavity or a deep tissue layer.
- **Second Intraoperative Count**: Executed as subcutaneous tissue closure commences.
- **Final Count**: Carried out during skin closure to ensure total accountability before the patient leaves the operating table.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Procedure for Manual Counting
headings.content: Executing a manual needle count requires disciplined physical mechanics to avoid errors. The scrub nurse and circulating nurse must count items in a set directional flow, typically moving from the sterile field to the Mayo stand and finally to the back table. Needles housed in a counted pack must be verified against the manufacturer label before opening. As needles are used, they are placed in a designated foam block, magnetic pad, or counted suture box. Broken needles require extreme caution; all fragments must be collected and pieced together to ensure nothing remains missing.

headings.title: Managing Discrepancies and Missing Needles
headings.content: Finding a count discrepancy halts all surgical progress immediately. The scrub nurse must alert the surgeon with a clear statement: "Count is incorrect." The entire surgical team stops wound closure, and a systematic search begins. The sterile field, Mayo stand, floor, linen hampers, and trash receptacles are meticulously checked. If the missing item is still unlocated, the circulating nurse informs the lead surgeon, and an intraoperative X-ray is ordered. Under no circumstances should the patient be transferred to the recovery room while an active count discrepancy remains unresolved.

headings.title: Documentation and Legal Implications
headings.content: Precise documentation safeguards both the patient and the healthcare institution. The nursing record must clearly state the exact counts performed at baseline, during closure phases, and at the end of the procedure. If a recount occurs due to an initial mismatch, this must also be logged with specific details. Legally, an undocumented count is legally considered an unperformed count in a court of law. Nurses must sign off on the nursing notes with their full names and designations, reflecting accountability for every sharp utilized during the surgical intervention.
